title: Mineralisation of Atmospheric Aerosol Particles and Trace Element Analysis by ICP-OES
author: Dufour, Migon
materials: ICP multi-element standard solution VIII CertiPUR®
mono-elemental solutions for V and Ti

steps.title: Prepare sample set
steps.instruction: Organize all natural aerosol and SRM samples into sets of 54, adding two blank filters and two reagent blanks to each set.

steps.title: Weigh reference material
steps.instruction: Weigh 10 mg of NIST 1648 and 1648a onto a filter using a Mettler Toledo XS205 precision balance.

steps.title: Load filters into Teflon bottles
steps.instruction: Fold each filter into quarters and place it into an acid‑cleaned Teflon bottle (60 mL capacity).

steps.title: Add acid digestion mixture
steps.instruction: Add the following acid mixture to each bottle: 1.5 mL HCl (30 % w/w), 0.5 mL HNO₃ (65 % w/w), and 0.5 mL HF (40 % w/w) (aqua regia + HF).

steps.title: Pre‑digestion sonication
steps.instruction: Place the set of bottles in an ultrasonic bath for 10 minutes.

steps.title: Block digestion
steps.instruction: Insert each Teflon bottle into the block digester, seal with a reflux condenser cap, and run the temperature program:

substeps.instruction: Ramp temperature at 2 °C min⁻¹ until reaching 130 °C.

steps.title: Post‑digestion residue treatment
steps.instruction: After cooling, dissolve the residue in 1.5 mL HNO₃ (65 %), sonicate for 15 minutes, then dilute to a final volume of 10 mL with Milli‑Q® water.

steps.title: Store final solution
steps.instruction: Transfer the solution to an acid‑cleaned polypropylene tube (15 mL) and store at 4 °C in a refrigerator until ICP‑OES analysis.

description: The analysis of atmospheric aerosol samples collected on filters may sometimes be a difficult challenge, owing to the combined effects of chemically resistant matrices potentially present in the atmospheric aerosol (alumino-silicates, oxides, sea-spray, organic compounds [1]), low quantities of collected material (of the order of few milligrammes, typically) and trace/ultra-trace elemental concentrations encountered (of the order of few μg L−1, typically). Attempts to totally digest these matrices with a single protocol may lead to signal losses, therefore yielding low recoveries and hence underestimated measurements. Non-destructive analytical techniques such as X-ray fluorescence, proton-induced X-ray emission (PIXE) are currently being developed which skip the mineralisation phase, but their detection limits are still too high given the elemental concentrations found in the atmospheric aerosol: below 100 ng m−3, the degree of overestimation by Energy Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (EDXRF) increases when concentrations decrease [2]. In addition, the non-uniformity of elemental distribution on filters may lead to erroneous results [3]. Therefore, mineralisation remains a crucial, and unavoidable phase in the preparation of natural particulate samples for elemental analysis. The present work proposes an alternative, tentatively all-purpose mineralisation protocol (the splitting of samples into sub-samples by cutting filters is banned because of the non-uniform distribution of matter [4]), followed by an analytical method specifically adapted to trace elements in atmospheric particulate samples. Digestion methods were validated by analysing SRM 1648 and 1648a samples. Results from this mineralisation method agree well with the certified values (Table 2), except for the case of As in SRM 1648a (recovery: 84%).
